title: Batch, Real-Time & Embedding Pipeline Design
scopeHtml: Scope: Batch queues with retries and dead-letter queues, streaming with backpressure, and idempotent embedding pipelines kept in sync with indexes.

notes.title: Three pipeline shapes in GenAI systems
notes.html:
What it is. A pipeline is a chain of steps that moves data from where it starts to where it is useful. GenAI systems need three different shapes, and mixing them up is the most common design mistake:

  1. Batch: lots of work, nobody is waiting. Example: summarise 2 million support tickets overnight. You care about total cost and finishing eventually, not about any single item's speed.
  2. Real-time (streaming): one user is waiting right now. Example: a chat answer appearing word by word. You care about time to first token and about not falling over when many users arrive at once.
  3. Embedding pipeline: a background process that turns documents into embeddings (a list of numbers, a vector, that captures meaning) and stores them in a vector index (a database that finds "similar meaning" fast). You care that the index always matches the source documents, even when the process crashes halfway.

Why they exist. An LLM call is slow (seconds), costly (priced per token, a token being a word piece of roughly 3 to 4 characters), rate-limited (providers cap requests and tokens per minute) and flaky (timeouts, 429 "too many requests", 5xx errors). Plain function calls do not survive that. Queues, retries and idempotent writes are the tools that make slow, costly, flaky calls safe.

How to choose.

Is a human waiting for this result?
  yes -> real-time path: stream tokens, small timeouts, shed load, backpressure
  no  -> can it wait minutes to hours?
          yes -> batch path: queue + workers + retries + DLQ (+ provider batch API for ~half price)
          no  -> near-real-time queue with autoscaled workers

Does the data feed a search index?
  yes -> embedding pipeline: idempotent writes, content hashes, versioned embeddings, delete handling

Real products. ChatGPT and Claude apps stream tokens over HTTP (real-time). OpenAI and Anthropic both offer asynchronous batch APIs at a discount for non-urgent work (verify current discount and window in the docs). Notion, Slack and GitHub search keep a vector or keyword index in sync with user edits through event streams and background workers (exact internals are not public; the pattern is standard).

Real life. A restaurant has a dine-in window (real-time: the customer is staring at you), a catering order system (batch: due tomorrow, do it cheaply in bulk) and a stock list that must match the shelves (embedding sync: the list must not lie).

Common interview traps.

  • Treating everything as a synchronous request: a 10-minute job inside an HTTP request will time out at a load balancer (often 30 to 60 seconds).
  • Saying "just use Kafka" without stating what guarantee you need (ordering, replay, at-least-once).
  • Forgetting that the three shapes have different success metrics: cost per item, time to first token, index freshness.

notes.title: Batch processing with queues
notes.html:
What it is. A queue is a line of jobs. Producers put jobs in; workers take them out and process them. If a worker dies, the job goes back in line. Producers and workers are decoupled, so a traffic spike makes the line longer instead of crashing the system.

Why it exists for GenAI. Provider rate limits are a hard ceiling. If you have 100,000 documents and a limit of, say, 50 requests per second (made-up number), you cannot fire them all. A queue lets a fixed pool of workers drain jobs at a speed the provider accepts. Also, a job that takes 8 seconds should not hold an HTTP connection open.

Step by step.

1. Producer writes job {id, payload} to the queue (and records id in a jobs table: status=QUEUED)
2. Worker receives the job; the queue hides it from other workers for a *visibility timeout* (e.g. 120 s)
3. Worker calls the LLM, validates the output, writes the result
4. Worker ACKs (deletes) the job from the queue; jobs table: status=DONE
5. If the worker crashes before ACK, the visibility timeout expires and the job reappears -> retried by another worker

Step 5 is why queues give at-least-once delivery: a job can run twice (the worker finished the work but died just before the ACK). So every worker step must be idempotent (safe to run twice with the same result). Exactly-once is practically built from at-least-once plus idempotency.

Sizing workers. By Little's law, concurrency = throughput x latency. To sustain 20 jobs/s when each job takes 4 s: 20 x 4 = 80 concurrent calls. If the provider allows only 50 concurrent, your ceiling is 50 / 4 = 12.5 jobs/s, and extra workers just earn more 429 errors.

Python (in-process worker pool with queue.Queue; production would use SQS, RabbitMQ, Redis streams, Kafka or Celery):

import queue, threading

jobs: "queue.Queue[dict]" = queue.Queue(maxsize=1000)   # bounded queue
results = {}

def worker():
    while True:
        job = jobs.get()
        try:
            results[job["id"]] = f"summary of {job['text'][:20]}"  # real code: call the LLM here
        finally:
            jobs.task_done()          # the "ACK"

for _ in range(8):
    threading.Thread(target=worker, daemon=True).start()
for i in range(20):
    jobs.put({"id": i, "text": f"document number {i}"})   # blocks when full: backpressure
jobs.join()
print(len(results))   # prints 20

Kotlin (coroutines and a bounded Channel):

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel

data class Job(val id: Int, val text: String)

fun main() = runBlocking {
    val jobs = Channel<Job>(capacity = 1000)          // bounded: send() suspends when full
    val results = java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<Int, String>()
    val workers = List(8) {
        launch(Dispatchers.IO) {
            for (job in jobs) results[job.id] = "summary of ${job.text.take(20)}" // call the LLM here
        }
    }
    repeat(20) { jobs.send(Job(it, "document number $it")) }
    jobs.close(); workers.joinAll()
    println(results.size)   // prints 20
}

Java (ArrayBlockingQueue with a thread pool):

import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class BatchDemo {
    record Job(int id, String text) {}
    public static void main(String[] a) throws Exception {
        BlockingQueue<Job> jobs = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1000);   // bounded
        ConcurrentHashMap<Integer, String> results = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);
        for (int w = 0; w < 8; w++) pool.submit(() -> {
            try {
                while (true) {
                    Job j = jobs.take();
                    if (j.id() < 0) return;                    // poison pill = stop
                    results.put(j.id(), "summary of " + j.text()); // call the LLM here
                }
            } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        });
        for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) jobs.put(new Job(i, "document number " + i)); // blocks when full
        for (int w = 0; w < 8; w++) jobs.put(new Job(-1, ""));
        pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(1, TimeUnit.MINUTES);
        System.out.println(results.size());   // prints 20
    }
}

Real tools. AWS SQS (visibility timeout, built-in DLQ), RabbitMQ (ack/nack), Kafka (consumer groups, offsets), Celery and Temporal (workflow engines that persist progress), Google Cloud Tasks. Spring users often use Spring Cloud Stream or SQS listeners.

Production failure patterns.

  • Visibility timeout shorter than the job: the job reappears while still running, two workers do it twice, you pay double. Set timeout above p99 duration, and extend it (heartbeat) for long jobs.
  • Unbounded queue: the producer outruns workers, memory or storage balloons. Bound it or alert on depth and age of oldest message.
  • Lost progress: a 6-hour job with no checkpointing restarts from zero. Split into small independent items.

Real life. A post office sorting room: letters arrive on a belt (queue), a fixed number of clerks sort them, and a letter nobody confirmed delivered goes back on the belt.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming "exactly-once delivery" from the queue; the honest answer is at-least-once plus idempotent handlers.
  • Scaling workers past the provider rate limit and calling it throughput.
  • Forgetting the visibility timeout, which causes duplicated, double-billed LLM calls.

notes.title: Retries, backoff and jitter
notes.html:
What it is. A retry re-runs a failed call. Exponential backoff waits longer after each failure (1 s, 2 s, 4 s...). Jitter adds randomness so that thousands of clients do not all retry at the same instant.

Why it exists. Most LLM failures are transient: HTTP 429 (rate limited), 500/502/503/529 (server trouble or overloaded; Anthropic uses 529 for overload, verify), timeouts, dropped connections. Waiting briefly usually fixes them. But retrying blindly causes a retry storm: the provider is struggling, all your clients retry together, the provider struggles more.

Which errors to retry.

Retry (transient):   429, 500, 502, 503, 504, 529, connection reset, read timeout
Do NOT retry:        400 invalid request, 401/403 auth, 404 wrong model id, content too long
                     (these fail identically every time - retrying burns time and money)
Retry carefully:     model output that fails your JSON validation (retry with a repair prompt, max 1-2 times)

The formula (full jitter). sleep = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)). With base 1 s, cap 30 s: attempt 0 sleeps up to 1 s, attempt 1 up to 2 s, attempt 2 up to 4 s, attempt 5 up to 30 s (32 capped to 30). If the server sends a Retry-After header, honour it instead.

Retry budget. Limit attempts (3 to 5) and total time. Also limit retries as a fraction of traffic (say 10 percent), otherwise retries multiply load exactly when the provider is weakest. Note that provider SDKs (including anthropic) already retry some errors by default with a configurable max_retries (verify exact defaults); do not stack your own retry loop on top without counting: 3 x 3 = 9 calls.

Python:

import random, time

RETRYABLE = {429, 500, 502, 503, 504, 529}

class LlmError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, status): self.status = status

def call_with_retry(fn, max_attempts=5, base=1.0, cap=30.0):
    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        try:
            return fn()
        except LlmError as e:
            if e.status not in RETRYABLE or attempt == max_attempts - 1:
                raise                               # permanent error or out of attempts
            time.sleep(random.uniform(0, min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt)))  # full jitter

# prints "ok" after two simulated 429s
calls = iter([429, 429, 200])
def flaky():
    s = next(calls)
    if s != 200: raise LlmError(s)
    return "ok"
print(call_with_retry(flaky, base=0.01))

Kotlin:

import kotlinx.coroutines.delay
import kotlin.random.Random

class LlmError(val status: Int) : Exception()
val retryable = setOf(429, 500, 502, 503, 504, 529)

suspend fun <T> withRetry(maxAttempts: Int = 5, baseMs: Long = 1000, capMs: Long = 30_000, block: suspend () -> T): T {
    var attempt = 0
    while (true) {
        try { return block() }
        catch (e: LlmError) {
            if (e.status !in retryable || ++attempt >= maxAttempts) throw e
            val ceiling = minOf(capMs, baseMs shl (attempt - 1))
            delay(Random.nextLong(0, ceiling + 1))      // full jitter
        }
    }
}
// returns the block's value, or rethrows after 5 attempts / on a non-retryable status

Java (plain; Resilience4j Retry with IntervalFunction.ofExponentialRandomBackoff is the library option, verify in its docs):

import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

public class Retry {
    static class LlmError extends RuntimeException { final int status; LlmError(int s){status=s;} }
    static final Set<Integer> RETRYABLE = Set.of(429, 500, 502, 503, 504, 529);

    static <T> T call(Supplier<T> fn, int maxAttempts, long baseMs, long capMs) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
            try { return fn.get(); }
            catch (LlmError e) {
                if (!RETRYABLE.contains(e.status) || attempt == maxAttempts - 1) throw e;
                long ceiling = Math.min(capMs, baseMs << attempt);
                Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(ceiling + 1)); // full jitter
            }
        }
    }
    // returns fn's value, or rethrows the last LlmError
}

Idempotency of the call itself. A retry after a timeout may mean the first call actually succeeded and you are billed twice. For tool calls with side effects (send email, charge card) pass an idempotency key so the receiver ignores duplicates. The LLM call itself has no side effects, so the cost is money only.

Real life. Redialling a busy phone line: you wait a bit longer each time, and a thousand friends redialling in the same second would just keep the line jammed, hence randomness.

Common interview traps.

  • Retrying 400-class errors (a malformed request will never succeed).
  • Backoff without jitter: synchronised clients create a thundering herd.
  • Nested retries (SDK x queue x gateway) multiplying into dozens of calls per job.
  • Retrying a non-idempotent tool call without an idempotency key.

notes.title: Dead-letter queues and poison messages
notes.html:
What it is. A dead-letter queue (DLQ) is a side queue where jobs go after failing too many times. A poison message is a job that can never succeed (for example a corrupt PDF that crashes the parser, or a prompt that always trips a safety filter).

Why it exists. Without a DLQ, a poison message is retried forever, wastes money on every LLM call, and can block the line behind it (head-of-line blocking in ordered queues). The DLQ parks it so healthy work flows, and keeps it for a human or a repair script.

How it works.

main queue --> worker --fail--> retry (attempt 2, 3 ...) --still failing at maxReceiveCount--> DLQ
                                                                                        |
                                              alert + dashboard <-- depth, oldest age --+
                                              inspect -> fix bug or data -> *redrive* back to main queue

Each job carries an attempt counter and the last error. SQS does this natively with maxReceiveCount on a redrive policy; RabbitMQ uses dead-letter exchanges; Kafka has no built-in DLQ, so you write to a topic.dlq yourself and commit the offset. Always store the original payload, the error class, the stack summary, the model id and the prompt version, so the failure is reproducible.

Classify before parking.

  • Transient (429, timeout): retry with backoff, DLQ only after budget is spent.
  • Permanent (bad input, schema violation after repairs): go straight to the DLQ, skip pointless retries.
  • Systemic (provider outage): do NOT flood the DLQ with 50,000 healthy jobs; use a circuit breaker that pauses the consumer, then let the queue back up and resume later.

Redrive carefully. After you fix the bug, move DLQ messages back. Because the handler is idempotent, replaying is safe. Redrive at a throttled rate, or you recreate the original overload.

Python (job runner with attempt counter and DLQ):

MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3
main, dlq = [], []

def process(job):
    if "corrupt" in job["text"]:
        raise ValueError("parser crash")          # permanent failure
    return job["text"].upper()

def run(job):
    try:
        return process(job)
    except ValueError as e:                       # permanent: park immediately
        dlq.append({**job, "error": repr(e)})
    except Exception as e:                        # transient: requeue until budget is spent
        job["attempts"] = job.get("attempts", 0) + 1
        (dlq if job["attempts"] >= MAX_ATTEMPTS else main).append({**job, "error": repr(e)})

run({"id": 1, "text": "hello"}); run({"id": 2, "text": "corrupt pdf"})
print(len(dlq), dlq[0]["id"])   # prints: 1 2

Kotlin:

data class Job(val id: Int, val text: String, val attempts: Int = 0)
class PermanentError(msg: String) : Exception(msg)

val main = ArrayDeque<Job>()
val dlq = mutableListOf<Pair<Job, String>>()
const val MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3

fun process(j: Job): String =
    if ("corrupt" in j.text) throw PermanentError("parser crash") else j.text.uppercase()

fun run(j: Job) {
    try { process(j) }
    catch (e: PermanentError) { dlq += j to e.toString() }            // park immediately
    catch (e: Exception) {
        val next = j.copy(attempts = j.attempts + 1)
        if (next.attempts >= MAX_ATTEMPTS) dlq += next to e.toString() else main.addLast(next)
    }
}
// run(Job(2, "corrupt pdf")) leaves dlq.size == 1

Java:

import java.util.*;

public class DlqDemo {
    record Job(int id, String text, int attempts) {}
    static class PermanentError extends RuntimeException { PermanentError(String m){super(m);} }
    static final int MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3;
    static Deque<Job> main = new ArrayDeque<>();
    static List<String> dlq = new ArrayList<>();

    static String process(Job j) {
        if (j.text().contains("corrupt")) throw new PermanentError("parser crash");
        return j.text().toUpperCase();
    }
    static void run(Job j) {
        try { process(j); }
        catch (PermanentError e) { dlq.add(j.id() + ": " + e.getMessage()); }   // park immediately
        catch (RuntimeException e) {
            Job next = new Job(j.id(), j.text(), j.attempts() + 1);
            if (next.attempts() >= MAX_ATTEMPTS) dlq.add(next.id() + ": " + e); else main.addLast(next);
        }
    }
    // run(new Job(2, "corrupt pdf", 0)) -> dlq.size() == 1
}

Production failure patterns. A DLQ nobody watches is a graveyard: alert on DLQ depth and age of the oldest message. Retention shorter than your on-call response time means messages vanish (SQS DLQs inherit the original message timestamp, so a 4-day retention can expire a message sooner than expected; verify). Storing full prompts with personal data in the DLQ is a privacy issue: apply the same retention and access controls as production data.

Real life. The "returned to sender" bin at the post office: the letter with a smudged address stops blocking the belt, and a person looks at it later.

Common interview traps.

  • Retrying poison messages forever (cost and head-of-line blocking).
  • Having a DLQ but no alarm and no redrive procedure.
  • Using the DLQ to hide a systemic outage instead of pausing with a circuit breaker.
  • Redriving at full speed and re-triggering the rate limit.

notes.title: Provider batch APIs and cost
notes.html:
What it is. Both Anthropic (Message Batches) and OpenAI (Batch API) let you submit many requests in one go, processed asynchronously, typically at a reduced price in exchange for waiting up to about 24 hours (verify current discount, window and size limits in the docs; at the time of writing the discount is around 50 percent). You do not hold connections: you submit, poll, then download results.

Why use it. It removes the need for you to build rate-limit-aware workers for pure offline work: evals, nightly classification, backfills, re-summarising an archive. Provider batches also usually have separate, higher rate limits than the real-time API (verify).

How it works.

1. Build requests: each has a custom_id (YOUR key) + the usual params (model, max_tokens, messages)
2. Create batch -> returns batch id, status "in_progress"
3. Poll (every 30-60 s, or less often) until processing_status == "ended"
4. Stream results: each line has custom_id + result type: succeeded | errored | canceled | expired
5. Join results to your records by custom_id; re-submit only the failed ones

Results can come back in any order, so custom_id is the only way to match. Make it deterministic (for example doc-123@prompt-v7) so that a re-run does not create duplicates, which is idempotency again.

Python (anthropic SDK; method names are from the Message Batches API, verify in the SDK docs):

import os, time, anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()   # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
docs = {"doc-1": "First text...", "doc-2": "Second text..."}

batch = client.messages.batches.create(requests=[
    {"custom_id": f"{doc_id}@v1",
     "params": {"model": "claude-haiku-5-5", "max_tokens": 200,
                "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": f"Summarise: {text}"}]}}
    for doc_id, text in docs.items()
])
while client.messages.batches.retrieve(batch.id).processing_status != "ended":
    time.sleep(60)
for item in client.messages.batches.results(batch.id):
    if item.result.type == "succeeded":
        print(item.custom_id, item.result.message.content[0].text[:40])
    else:
        print(item.custom_id, "needs retry:", item.result.type)   # errored / expired / canceled

Kotlin and Java: the Java SDK com.anthropic:anthropic-java mirrors the same flow (create a batch, poll, iterate results); exact builder class names differ by SDK version, so verify them in the SDK docs rather than copy them from here. In a Spring or Kotlin service the usual pattern is: a scheduled job submits the batch and stores batch.id in a table, another scheduled job polls open batch ids, and a completion handler writes the results idempotently keyed by custom_id.

Trade-off table.

                  Own queue + workers          Provider batch API
Latency           seconds to minutes           up to ~24 h (verify)
Price             standard                     discounted (verify)
Control           retries, priority, partial   all-or-nothing submit, per-item result
Best for          mixed priority, SLA < 1 h    nightly evals, backfills, bulk labelling

Production failure patterns. Expired items (not finished in the window) must be resubmitted: track them. Very large prompt prefixes repeated in every request benefit from prompt caching together with batches (verify combined behaviour). Do not poll every second; you only add noise.

Real life. Dropping a big laundry load at a service wash: cheaper, picked up tomorrow, and you match your shirts to the ticket numbers (custom_id).

Common interview traps.

  • Using the batch API for anything interactive.
  • Assuming results arrive in submission order.
  • Not making custom_id deterministic, so a restart double-submits and double-pays.
  • Quoting a discount or limit as a fixed fact without saying "verify".

notes.title: Real-time processing: streaming tokens
notes.html:
What it is. Streaming means the server sends the answer in small pieces as the model produces them, instead of one big response at the end. The unit is usually a token or a small group of tokens, delivered as Server-Sent Events (SSE): a long-lived HTTP response with lines like data: {...}.

Why it exists. A model emits roughly tens of tokens per second. A 500-token answer can take around 10 seconds (illustrative). Waiting 10 s for a blank screen feels broken; seeing the first words after under a second feels instant. The key metrics:

TTFT  (time to first token)  = network + queueing + prompt processing ("prefill")  -> what the user *feels*
TPOT  (time per output token) = decode speed                                       -> reading speed
Total time ~= TTFT + (output_tokens x TPOT)
Example: TTFT 0.6 s, TPOT 25 ms, 400 tokens -> 0.6 + 400 x 0.025 = 0.6 + 10 = 10.6 s total,
         but the user starts reading at 0.6 s.

How it works end to end.

Browser/Android --HTTP--> Your backend --SSE stream--> LLM provider
   <---- SSE events <----   (relay each chunk)   <---- message_start, content_block_delta*, message_stop

Anthropic streams named events such as message_start, content_block_delta (which carries a text delta) and message_stop (verify event names in the docs). The SDKs wrap this in an iterator so you rarely parse SSE by hand.

Python (backend relaying a stream; anthropic SDK stream helper):

import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def stream_answer(question: str):
    with client.messages.stream(
        model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=400,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
    ) as stream:
        for text in stream.text_stream:       # yields small text deltas as they arrive
            yield text                         # e.g. wrap in "data: ...\n\n" for SSE

for piece in stream_answer("Explain DLQs in one sentence."):
    print(piece, end="", flush=True)           # prints the answer progressively

Kotlin (Android client consuming your own backend's SSE with OkHttp; never call the model with an API key from the app):

import okhttp3.*
import okhttp3.sse.*

val client = OkHttpClient()
val request = Request.Builder().url("https://api.example.com/chat/stream?q=hello").build()

val listener = object : EventSourceListener() {
    override fun onEvent(es: EventSource, id: String?, type: String?, data: String) {
        // append `data` to the UI state on the main thread (e.g. via StateFlow)
    }
    override fun onFailure(es: EventSource, t: Throwable?, response: Response?) { /* show retry */ }
}
EventSources.createFactory(client).newEventSource(request, listener)  // needs okhttp-sse artifact

Java (Spring MVC server side, exposing the stream; SseEmitter is a real Spring class):

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.mvc.method.annotation.SseEmitter;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

@RestController
public class ChatController {
    @GetMapping("/chat/stream")
    public SseEmitter stream(@RequestParam String q) {
        SseEmitter emitter = new SseEmitter(60_000L);       // 60 s timeout
        Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().submit(() -> {   // Java 21+
            try {
                for (String piece : new String[]{"Hello", " ", "world"}) {   // replace with provider stream
                    emitter.send(piece);                     // one SSE event per chunk
                }
                emitter.complete();
            } catch (Exception e) { emitter.completeWithError(e); }
        });
        return emitter;
    }
}

Production failure patterns.

  • Proxy buffering: nginx or a CDN buffers the response and the user sees nothing until the end. Disable buffering (X-Accel-Buffering: no for nginx) and send periodic comment heartbeats so idle timeouts do not cut the stream.
  • Client disconnects: the user closes the tab but the backend keeps pulling tokens and you pay for output nobody reads. Detect the disconnect and cancel the upstream request.
  • Mid-stream failure: the provider errors after 200 tokens. The HTTP status was already 200, so send an explicit error event and let the client offer retry or resume.
  • Moderation of partial output: you cannot unsend tokens; buffer sentence-sized chunks if output filtering is required.

Real life. A live radio commentary versus waiting for the written match report: the information is identical, but one starts being useful straight away.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimising total latency when the user feels TTFT.
  • Forgetting that errors after the first byte cannot change the HTTP status.
  • Not cancelling the upstream call when the client leaves.
  • Putting the provider API key in the mobile app instead of proxying.

notes.title: Backpressure and load shedding
notes.html:
What it is. Backpressure is how a slow consumer tells a fast producer "slow down". Without it, the fast side keeps piling data into memory until something breaks. Load shedding means deliberately rejecting some requests early so the rest still succeed.

Why it exists for GenAI. LLM calls are the slowest link in the chain. If your API accepts 1,000 requests per second but the model layer only completes 100 per second, then 900 per second pile up. With 10 s per request that is thousands of open connections, exhausted threads, memory growth and finally a crash that fails everybody, including requests that would have succeeded.

The three places backpressure appears.

  1. Producer to queue: a bounded queue; when full, put blocks or fails. (Used in the batch examples above.)
  2. Server to slow client while streaming: if the phone on a bad network reads slowly, tokens buffer on your server. Use reactive streams (Reactor Flux with onBackpressureBuffer(limit) or onBackpressureDrop, Kotlin Flow with buffer(capacity) and conflate()), and cap per-connection buffer size; disconnect clients that fall too far behind.
  3. Your service to the provider: a concurrency limiter (semaphore) sized to the provider limit, plus rate limiting by tokens per minute, not just requests per minute. A request with 30,000 input tokens counts far more than one with 300.

Policies when full (choose deliberately).

Block the producer      -> works inside one process; hides overload from callers
Reject fast (HTTP 429 / 503 + Retry-After) -> best for user-facing APIs; the client backs off
Drop oldest / drop newest -> fine for "latest wins" data (live typing suggestions), wrong for billing events
Degrade                 -> smaller model, shorter max_tokens, skip reranking, serve cached answer
Priority lanes          -> paying or interactive traffic ahead of batch jobs

Little's law again. In-flight = arrival rate x latency. At 100 requests/s and 10 s each, in-flight is 100 x 10 = 1,000. If your limiter allows 200, then 800 are waiting; the queue wait grows without bound unless arrivals fall below 20 per second (200 / 10) or you shed. A queue only absorbs a burst; it cannot fix a sustained rate above capacity.

Python (semaphore limiter plus fast rejection):

import asyncio

limit = asyncio.Semaphore(20)          # max 20 concurrent LLM calls
MAX_WAITING = 50
waiting = 0

async def handle(req_id: int):
    global waiting
    if waiting >= MAX_WAITING:
        return (503, "busy, retry later")        # shed load instead of queueing forever
    waiting += 1
    try:
        async with limit:
            waiting -= 1
            await asyncio.sleep(0.1)             # stand-in for the LLM call
            return (200, f"answer {req_id}")
    except BaseException:
        raise

async def main():
    out = await asyncio.gather(*(handle(i) for i in range(100)))
    print(sum(1 for s, _ in out if s == 503), "rejected")   # prints a positive number

asyncio.run(main())

Kotlin (Flow with a bounded buffer and limited concurrency):

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*

suspend fun main() = coroutineScope {
    (1..100).asFlow()
        .buffer(capacity = 50, onBufferOverflow = kotlinx.coroutines.channels.BufferOverflow.SUSPEND)
        .flatMapMerge(concurrency = 20) { id ->            // at most 20 LLM calls in flight
            flow { delay(100); emit("answer $id") }          // stand-in for the LLM call
        }
        .collect { println(it) }
}
// For streaming to a slow UI use .buffer(64) or .conflate() depending on whether every token matters.

Java (Resilience4j-style bulkhead idea with a plain Semaphore, no extra library):

import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;

public class Limiter {
    static final Semaphore inFlight = new Semaphore(20);
    static String handle(int id) throws InterruptedException {
        if (!inFlight.tryAcquire()) return "503 busy, retry later";   // shed immediately, never queue forever
        try { Thread.sleep(100); return "200 answer " + id; }         // stand-in for the LLM call
        finally { inFlight.release(); }
    }
}

Production failure patterns. Timeouts missing at any layer turn overload into a pile-up of zombie requests. Retries from clients during overload double the load (see backoff). An autoscaler that adds workers when the provider is the bottleneck just spends more and gets more 429s. Metrics to watch: queue depth, p95 queue wait, rejected count, in-flight calls, tokens per minute versus the quota.

Real life. A busy club with a doorman: when the room is full, people wait outside or are told to come back later. Letting everyone in would make the fire marshal close the venue.

Common interview traps.

  • "Just add a bigger queue": it converts an outage into long hidden latency.
  • Limiting requests per second but not tokens per minute.
  • No timeout on the LLM call, so slots never free up.
  • Dropping data that must not be dropped (use block or reject, not drop).

notes.title: Embedding pipelines: from document to vector
notes.html:
What it is. An embedding is a fixed-length list of numbers (for example 1,024 floats) produced by an embedding model so that texts with similar meaning land close together. An embedding pipeline turns your source documents into those vectors and stores them with metadata in a vector index (pgvector, Qdrant, Pinecone, OpenSearch, FAISS), so a RAG (retrieval-augmented generation, i.e. fetching relevant text to put in the prompt) system can search by meaning. See also: other C-track notes on RAG for retrieval quality; this section covers only the operational pipeline.

Why it is hard. The source data changes constantly (edits, deletes, permission changes), the embedding model is slow and rate limited, and the pipeline fails halfway. The goal is a consistent index: every live source chunk has exactly one correct vector, and no vector exists for deleted or outdated text.

Pipeline stages.

source change event (created/updated/deleted)
   -> fetch document + parse (PDF/HTML/text)
   -> split into chunks (e.g. ~500 tokens with ~50 overlap)
   -> for each chunk: content_hash = sha256(chunk_text + model_id + chunk_params)
   -> skip chunks whose (chunk_id, content_hash) already exist  <- saves most of the cost
   -> embed the new/changed chunks in batches (e.g. 64-256 per call)
   -> upsert vectors + metadata {doc_id, chunk_id, content_hash, model_id, version, acl}
   -> delete vectors of chunks that no longer exist in the document
   -> record the document's indexed_version

Deterministic IDs are the heart of it. Use chunk_id = f"{doc_id}:{chunk_index}" (or a hash of position and doc), not a random UUID. Then writing the same chunk twice overwrites instead of duplicating: that is idempotency. A random UUID per run means a retry leaves two copies and your search returns duplicates.

Numbers. 1,000,000 chunks x 1,024 dimensions x 4 bytes (float32) = 4,096,000,000 bytes, about 4.1 GB just for raw vectors, before the index graph overhead (HNSW, a common index type, often adds notable extra; verify for your store). If a document is edited and only 2 of 40 chunks changed, hashing means 2 embedding calls instead of 40, a 95 percent saving on that update.

Python (hash-based idempotent sync with a fake embedder and an in-memory "index"):

import hashlib

MODEL = "embed-v1"
index = {}   # chunk_id -> {"hash":..., "vec":...}   (stand-in for pgvector/Qdrant)

def embed(texts):                       # real code: call the embedding API in batches
    return [[float(len(t))] for t in texts]

def sync_document(doc_id, chunks):
    wanted = {}
    for i, text in enumerate(chunks):
        cid = f"{doc_id}:{i}"
        wanted[cid] = (text, hashlib.sha256(f"{MODEL}|{text}".encode()).hexdigest())
    todo = [cid for cid, (t, h) in wanted.items() if index.get(cid, {}).get("hash") != h]
    vecs = embed([wanted[c][0] for c in todo])
    for cid, v in zip(todo, vecs):
        index[cid] = {"hash": wanted[cid][1], "vec": v}          # upsert: safe to repeat
    stale = [c for c in index if c.startswith(f"{doc_id}:") and c not in wanted]
    for c in stale: del index[c]                                  # remove chunks that vanished
    return len(todo), len(stale)

print(sync_document("d1", ["a", "bb", "ccc"]))    # (3, 0)
print(sync_document("d1", ["a", "bb", "ccc"]))    # (0, 0)  second run does nothing
print(sync_document("d1", ["a", "BB"]))           # (1, 1)  one re-embedded, one deleted

Kotlin:

import java.security.MessageDigest

const val MODEL = "embed-v1"
data class Entry(val hash: String, val vec: List<Float>)
val index = mutableMapOf<String, Entry>()                 // stand-in for pgvector/Qdrant

fun sha256(s: String) = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
    .digest(s.toByteArray()).joinToString("") { "%02x".format(it) }

fun embed(texts: List<String>) = texts.map { listOf(it.length.toFloat()) }   // real code: API call

fun syncDocument(docId: String, chunks: List<String>): Pair<Int, Int> {
    val wanted = chunks.mapIndexed { i, t -> "$docId:$i" to (t to sha256("$MODEL|$t")) }.toMap()
    val todo = wanted.filter { (id, p) -> index[id]?.hash != p.second }.keys.toList()
    embed(todo.map { wanted.getValue(it).first }).forEachIndexed { i, v ->
        index[todo[i]] = Entry(wanted.getValue(todo[i]).second, v)        // upsert
    }
    val stale = index.keys.filter { it.startsWith("$docId:") && it !in wanted }
    stale.forEach { index.remove(it) }
    return todo.size to stale.size
}
// syncDocument("d1", listOf("a","bb","ccc")) -> (3, 0); running it again -> (0, 0)

Java:

import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.util.*;

public class EmbedSync {
    static final String MODEL = "embed-v1";
    record Entry(String hash, float[] vec) {}
    static final Map<String, Entry> index = new HashMap<>();   // stand-in for pgvector/Qdrant

    static String sha256(String s) throws Exception {
        byte[] d = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(s.getBytes());
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (byte b : d) sb.append(String.format("%02x", b));
        return sb.toString();
    }
    static float[] embed(String t) { return new float[]{t.length()}; }   // real code: API call, batched

    static int[] sync(String docId, List<String> chunks) throws Exception {
        Map<String, String> hashes = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < chunks.size(); i++) hashes.put(docId + ":" + i, sha256(MODEL + "|" + chunks.get(i)));
        int embedded = 0, deleted = 0, i = 0;
        for (var e : hashes.entrySet()) {
            Entry old = index.get(e.getKey());
            if (old == null || !old.hash().equals(e.getValue())) {
                index.put(e.getKey(), new Entry(e.getValue(), embed(chunks.get(i)))); embedded++;  // upsert
            }
            i++;
        }
        deleted = (int) index.keySet().stream()
            .filter(k -> k.startsWith(docId + ":") && !hashes.containsKey(k)).count();
        index.keySet().removeIf(k -> k.startsWith(docId + ":") && !hashes.containsKey(k));
        return new int[]{embedded, deleted};   // second identical run returns {0, 0}
    }
}

Real tools. LangChain's indexing API with a RecordManager tracks hashes to skip unchanged documents and clean up old ones (verify current names), LlamaIndex has ingestion pipelines with document-hash caches, Qdrant and pgvector support upserts by ID natively (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE in Postgres), and Spring AI VectorStore exposes add and delete (verify id semantics per store).

Real life. A library catalogue that is updated by comparing each book's barcode: only new or changed books get re-labelled, and withdrawn books are removed from the shelf list.

Common interview traps.

  • Random UUID chunk ids, which duplicate chunks on every retry.
  • Hashing only the text and forgetting model id and chunking parameters, so a config change silently leaves stale vectors.
  • Embedding chunk by chunk (one API call each) instead of batching.
  • Ignoring that embeddings from different models are not comparable.

notes.title: Keeping the index in sync: deletes, ordering and the outbox
notes.html:
What it is. Index synchronization is making the vector index reflect the source of truth (your database or document store) over time. The index is a derived copy: if it is wrong you can rebuild it, so the source must always win.

Where it goes wrong.

  1. Dual-write problem: your code updates the database and then calls the indexer. If the process dies in between, the two disagree forever. There is no atomic transaction across a database and a vector store.
  2. Out-of-order events: edit 1 and edit 2 are processed by two workers; edit 2 finishes first, then edit 1 overwrites it with older content. Result: stale index.
  3. Missed deletes: polling "what changed since" misses deleted rows, so removed or permission-revoked documents stay searchable. This is a security bug, not just a quality bug.
  4. Partial failures: some chunks of a document updated, some not, so retrieval sees a mix of old and new text.

Fix 1, the transactional outbox. Write the business change and an outbox row in the same database transaction. A separate relay (a poller, or Debezium change data capture reading the database log) publishes outbox rows to the queue. The change is either fully recorded or not at all, and the event is delivered at least once (so the consumer must be idempotent).

BEGIN;  UPDATE documents SET body=..., version=version+1 WHERE id=42;
        INSERT INTO outbox(doc_id, version, op) VALUES (42, 7, 'upsert');  COMMIT;
relay -> queue -> embedding worker -> vector index

Fix 2, version guards. Every event carries the source version (or updated_at). The worker only writes if its version is greater than or equal to the one in the index. Postgres example idea: ... ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE ... WHERE excluded.version > chunks.version. A late, older event becomes a harmless no-op. Per-document ordering can also come from partitioning a Kafka topic by doc_id.

Fix 3, tombstones for deletes. Treat delete as an event (op='delete') and keep a soft-delete marker until the index confirms removal. Filter retrieval by an active flag or acl metadata as a second defence.

Fix 4, reconciliation. Even good pipelines drift. A nightly job compares counts and (doc_id, version) between source and index, repairs differences, and reports a drift rate. Treat it as a safety net, not as the main mechanism.

Fix 5, atomic visibility with versions or aliases. For a full re-embed (new model or new chunking), build a new collection docs_v2 in the background, verify recall on a test set, then switch an alias or config flag from docs_v1 to docs_v2. Roll back by flipping the alias. Never mix vectors from two embedding models in one collection, because distances between them are meaningless. Dual-write new changes to both collections during the migration.

Python (version-guarded upsert, applied idempotently):

index = {}   # chunk_id -> {"version": int, "text": str}

def apply_event(ev):
    cur = index.get(ev["chunk_id"])
    if ev["op"] == "delete":
        if cur is None or cur["version"] <= ev["version"]:
            index[ev["chunk_id"]] = {"version": ev["version"], "text": None}   # tombstone
        return
    if cur is None or cur["version"] < ev["version"]:      # older/duplicate events are ignored
        index[ev["chunk_id"]] = {"version": ev["version"], "text": ev["text"]}

apply_event({"chunk_id": "d1:0", "version": 2, "op": "upsert", "text": "new"})
apply_event({"chunk_id": "d1:0", "version": 1, "op": "upsert", "text": "old"})  # arrives late
print(index["d1:0"]["text"])    # prints: new

Kotlin:

data class Ev(val chunkId: String, val version: Int, val op: String, val text: String? = null)
data class Row(val version: Int, val text: String?)
val index = mutableMapOf<String, Row>()

fun apply(ev: Ev) {
    val cur = index[ev.chunkId]
    if (ev.op == "delete") {
        if (cur == null || cur.version <= ev.version) index[ev.chunkId] = Row(ev.version, null) // tombstone
        return
    }
    if (cur == null || cur.version < ev.version) index[ev.chunkId] = Row(ev.version, ev.text)
}
// apply(Ev("d1:0", 2, "upsert", "new")); apply(Ev("d1:0", 1, "upsert", "old")) -> text stays "new"

Java:

import java.util.*;

public class VersionGuard {
    record Ev(String chunkId, int version, String op, String text) {}
    record Row(int version, String text) {}
    static final Map<String, Row> index = new HashMap<>();

    static void apply(Ev ev) {
        Row cur = index.get(ev.chunkId());
        if (ev.op().equals("delete")) {
            if (cur == null || cur.version() <= ev.version()) index.put(ev.chunkId(), new Row(ev.version(), null));
            return;
        }
        if (cur == null || cur.version() < ev.version()) index.put(ev.chunkId(), new Row(ev.version(), ev.text()));
    }
    // apply(new Ev("d1:0", 2, "upsert", "new")); apply(new Ev("d1:0", 1, "upsert", "old")); -> still "new"
}

Real products. Debezium (CDC) feeding Kafka then an indexer is a standard recipe for Elasticsearch and vector stores; Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY or logical replication suit smaller systems; pgvector keeps vectors in the same database as the rows, which removes the dual-write problem entirely for many apps (a strong, simple default to mention in interviews); Elasticsearch and OpenSearch use external versioning (version_type=external) for exactly the stale-write case (verify in docs).

Real life. Two accountants editing a ledger copy: each entry has a page number (version), a late photocopy of an old page does not replace a newer page, and a monthly audit compares the copy with the original.

Common interview traps.

  • Writing to the database and the index in two separate calls and hoping.
  • Forgetting deletes and permission changes, leaking documents a user may no longer see.
  • Mixing two embedding models in the same collection during a gradual migration.
  • Using wall-clock timestamps for ordering across machines (clock skew); prefer a monotonically increasing version.

notes.title: Failure patterns, observability and runbook
notes.html:
What it is. The practices that keep the three pipelines healthy after launch: measure, alert, and know what to do when it breaks.

Metrics per pipeline.

Batch:      queue depth, age of oldest message, success rate, retries per job, DLQ depth/age, cost per item,
            tokens per minute vs quota, job duration p50/p95/p99
Real-time:  TTFT p50/p95, tokens/s, error rate by status, in-flight calls, rejected (429/503) count,
            client disconnects, stream abort rate
Embedding:  index lag (now - source_updated_at for the newest unindexed change), drift rate from reconciliation,
            chunks embedded per hour, skip ratio from hashes, delete backlog, embed API error rate

Typical incidents and first moves.

Symptom Likely cause First action
Queue depth climbs, workers idle Provider 429s, workers backing off Check quota, lower concurrency, do not add workers
Bill jumps overnight Visibility timeout too short or retry loop, double processing Check duplicate custom_ids, attempts per job
Chat shows nothing, then everything Proxy buffering Disable buffering, check SSE headers
Search returns deleted documents Missed delete events Run reconciliation, add tombstones, filter by active
Search quality drops after "no change" Mixed embedding models or chunk params in one collection Compare model_id metadata, reindex into new collection
DLQ fills with one error Systemic bug or outage Fix cause, pause consumer, throttled redrive
Memory climbs on the streaming server Slow clients, unbounded buffers Bound buffers, disconnect laggards

Design checklist (use this in interviews).

  1. State who is waiting, so pick batch or real-time.
  2. Queue between producer and workers, bounded, with a visibility timeout above p99.
  3. Retries only for transient errors, exponential backoff with full jitter, a retry budget.
  4. DLQ with attempt counter, alarms, and a throttled redrive process.
  5. Concurrency limit equal to the provider quota; shed or degrade when full.
  6. Deterministic IDs and content hashes so every write is idempotent.
  7. Outbox plus version guard plus tombstones for sync; nightly reconciliation as a net.
  8. Versioned collections and alias switch for model or chunking changes.
  9. Metrics, structured logs with job_id, custom_id, model_id, prompt_version, and a runbook.

Cost guard. Set a per-job and per-day token budget with a hard stop, because a retry bug in a loop can spend real money quickly. Log token usage from each response (usage fields) to a metrics store and alert on spend rate, not only on error rate.

Real life. A hospital ward: monitors (metrics), an escalation list (runbook), a quarantine room for cases that cannot be treated now (DLQ) and a daily round comparing charts with reality (reconciliation).

Common interview traps.

  • Alerting on error rate only; the dangerous failures are silent (stale index, double billing, slow drift).
  • No way to replay: logs without payloads or versions make incidents unreproducible.
  • Promising "zero downtime reindex" without an alias switch and rollback path.
  • Mentioning tools (Kafka, Temporal) instead of the guarantees they provide.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Pick the shape by who is waiting: batch (cost, eventual), real-time (TTFT, load), embedding (consistency).
  • Batch: bounded queue, workers sized by Little's law and the provider quota, at-least-once delivery so handlers must be idempotent, visibility timeout above p99.
  • Retries: only transient errors (429, 5xx, timeouts), exponential backoff with full jitter, honour Retry-After, cap attempts, and never stack retry layers blindly.
  • DLQ: attempt counter, classify transient versus permanent versus systemic, alarm on depth and age, redrive slowly after the fix; use a circuit breaker for outages.
  • Provider batch APIs trade latency (up to about a day) for lower price; match results by deterministic custom_id; verify discount and limits.
  • Streaming: users feel TTFT; SSE relay, disable proxy buffering, cancel upstream on disconnect, handle errors after the first byte explicitly.
  • Backpressure: bounded buffers, concurrency limiter, token-aware rate limiting, shed or degrade instead of queueing forever.
  • Embedding pipelines: deterministic chunk ids, content hash including model and chunk params, batch embedding, upsert plus delete of stale chunks.
  • Sync: transactional outbox or CDC, version guards, tombstones, nightly reconciliation, new collection plus alias switch for model changes, and never mix embedding models.
  • Observe queue age, DLQ depth, TTFT, index lag and spend; keep payloads and versions so incidents can be replayed.
